newsitem.title: JAPAN: Drought hits North Korea, threatens harvest-report.
newsitem.headline: Drought hits North Korea, threatens harvest-report.

text.p: Famine-struck North Korea, hit by two years of flooding that destroyed much of its harvest, is now facing the threat of drought in some areas, official media reported on Sunday.
The Tokyo-based Radiopress news agency quoted Radio Pyongyang as saying a major drought had hit four of North Korea's nine provinces and was threatening agricultural production.
"The drought is exceptional... If there is no rain there may be serious damage to agricultural production," Radiopress quoted the official radio as saying.
North Korea, which has long proclaimed a policy of self-reliance, has been forced to plea for aid from major countries to avoid a famine.
The drought had affected Whanghaepuk and Pyongyang provinces in the southwest and Hamkyongnam and Hankyongpuk provinces in the northeast of the country, Radiopress quoted Pyongyang radio as saying.
Nampo in the southeast had been suffering from drought for almost a month, the report said.
The monitoring agency also quoted the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) as saying troops had been drafted in to draw water from wells, hot springs and reservoirs to combat the drought.
"(Soldiers) are rising to the task of combatting the exceptional drought," KCNA reported.
The drought was due to unusually hot weather along North Korea's west coast, Radiopress quoted Radio Pyongyang as saying.

North Korea is suffering from widespread famine caused by floods that devastated much of the country's farmland and industrial bases in 1995 and 1996 and exacerbated Pyongyang's already severe food shortages.

Despite repeated United Nations World Food Programme appeals for aid and bilateral donations from governments and aid groups, North Korea still needed to import at least 400,000 tonnes of grain to maintain daily rations at the minimum 460 grams (one pound) until the next harvest in October, South Korea said last week.
